Law of Supply

Law of Supply

Everything else being equal, when the price of a good increases, the quantity supplied of the good increases…

And when the price of a good decreases, the quantity supplied of that good decreases.

ECON 104
08

Defining terms

  • Supply is the seller’s willingness/ability to produce/provide a good/service.
  • The supply curve shows the relationship between quantity of a good supplied at different prices.
  • The quantity supplied is the amount of a good that a seller is willing/able to produce/provide at a particular price.

Supply curve of Diet Coke on campus

ECON 104
10

Moving along the curve

  • As price changes, we move along our supply curve.
  • These changes are referred to as changes in quantity supplied…
Note: these are NOT changes in supply!
ECON 104
11

Why does the supply curve slope up?

  • As price increases, it becomes more worth it to put in more effort to produce.
  • The opportunity cost of not supplying increases!

Another way of thinking about supply

  • Assume I already have 12 diet coke cans with me.
  • You want to buy one from me.
  • My lowest-valued use is to drink it to quench my thirst — I’m willing to sell it for $1.
  • Now, if you have bought 11 diet cokes from me, and now want to buy the 12th one…
  • The diet coke you want to buy from me, I would drink with my Biryani, which I value very much. So, you need to give me at least $6 to buy it from me.

Another way to think about supply

Demand Curve for Diet Coke
Supply Curve for Diet Coke
The gap between my 12-can inventory and how many I want to keep for myself, at each price, is how many I’m willing to sell — and that traces out an upward-sloping supply curve.

Producer Surplus

ECON 104

Producer Surplus

  • We noted that a buyer enters into an exchange only if they expect to benefit.
  • How do we model how much a seller benefits?
Producer surplus

The difference between the maximum willingness to accept and the price actually received, for all units sold.

ECON 104
17

Graphing producer surplus

  • Assume the price of Diet Coke is $4.
  • Producer surplus is the area under the price level and above the supply curve.
ECON 104
18

Different producers have different producer surpluses

  • The blue is the total producer surplus.
  • Low-cost producers have more producer surplus.
  • High-cost producers have less.
Cowen & Tabarrok, Modern Principles: Macroeconomics, Figure 3.10.

Shifting the supply curve

Supply and costs

  1. To reiterate, supply is closely connected with cost.
  2. A shift in the supply curve means that producers are willing to supply greater or lesser quantities at the same price than before…
  3. Or, they are willing to accept a higher or lower price for supplying the same quantity as before.

What shifts supply?

Costs! What affects costs?

  1. Technological innovations
  2. Changes in the price of inputs
  3. Expectations
  4. Entry or exit by other producers
  5. Changes in opportunity cost
ECON 104
24

Changes in Input Prices

  • When input prices rise, firms supply less of the final product.
    • Supply shifts left.
  • When input prices fall, firms supply more of the final product.
    • Supply shifts right.
Example: What happens to the supply of coffee if the price of coffee beans (a key input) rises?
It costs the coffee shop more to make each cup, so they supply fewer cups at every price — and if bean prices fall, they can profitably supply more.
ECON 104
25

Changes in technology (innovation!)

  • Technology allows firms to transform inputs into final goods.
  • Advances in technology increase supply.
    • The curve shifts to the right.
  • Losses of technology decrease supply.
    • The curve shifts to the left.
Example: A coffee shop gets a faster espresso machine. What happens to supply?
It can serve more drinks at the same cost, so supply increases — but if that machine breaks down, they can serve fewer, so supply decreases.
ECON 104
26

Changes in expectations

  • People’s expectations about the future will impact their actions today.
  • If producers expect price to increase in the future, they will supply less today.
    • Curve shifts to the left.
  • If producers expect price to decrease in the future, they will supply more today.
    • Curve shifts to the right.
Example: A gas station expects gas prices to rise next week. What happens to supply today?
They hold back some gas today to sell later at the higher price, so supply decreases today — if they expected prices to fall instead, they’d sell as much as they can right now.
ECON 104
27

Number of sellers (entry or exit)

  • Market supply largely depends on how many sellers are in a market.
  • If more sellers enter a market, there is more supply!
    • The curve shifts to the right.
  • If sellers retire or leave a market, there is less supply.
    • The curve shifts to the left.
Example: The university issues more licenses to set up food trucks on campus. What happens to market supply?
More sellers enter the market, so market supply increases — and if licenses are pulled back instead, market supply decreases.
ECON 104
28

Changes in opportunity cost!

  • If your opportunity cost increases (you could be doing more profitable things with your time and resources), supply of the good decreases.
    • The curve shifts to the left.
  • And vice versa!
Example: A farmer can plant either corn or soybeans on his land. If soybean prices rise sharply, what happens to the supply of corn?
Growing corn now has a higher opportunity cost — the farmer gives up more valuable soybeans — so the supply of corn decreases — and if soybean prices fall, corn supply increases.

Practice: Will Supply Increase or Decrease?

The price of lumber rises sharply. What happens to the supply of new furniture?
A new 3D-printing process lets manufacturers produce sneakers faster and cheaper. What happens to supply?
Home builders expect the price of lumber to fall next year. What happens to the supply of new houses this year?
Several small bakeries in town close down. What happens to the market supply of bread?
ECON 104
30

Practice: Supply, or Quantity Supplied?

The price of sneakers itself rises. What happens to quantity supplied of sneakers?
A baker could earn more money working as a chef at a restaurant instead. What happens to the supply of bread?
New regulations require costly safety upgrades at furniture factories. What happens to the supply of furniture?
The price of bread itself falls. What happens to quantity supplied of bread?
ECON 104
31

Overview

  • The law of supply: all else equal, if the price of a good increases, the quantity supplied of that good increases.
  • Supply curves slope up — sellers need a higher price to be willing to supply more.
  • Producer surplus is the seller’s gain from trade: the area above the supply curve and below the price.
  • Shifts in the supply curve come from changes in cost: technology, input prices, expectations, the number of sellers, and opportunity cost.
